consensus_summary: Biblical 'knowing' (yada/ginōskō) primarily denotes intimate, experiential, covenantal relationship (esp. with God)—personal communion, love, and fidelity—rather than detached intellectual awareness; sexual union, election/foreknowledge, and obedience are treated as context-specific expressions of this core.
book_summary: Knowing is covenant relationship recognized and proven by faithful obedience, extending from marital intimacy to acknowledgment by one's covenant Lord; it is not mere mental assent or awareness (opposite: stranger).
book_core_identification: Covenant relationship recognized and proven by faithful obedience (marital to Lord's acknowledgment; not mere assent)
boundary_disagreement: Book makes recognition/proof by faithful obedience definitional to the core, potentially excluding pure relational or elective senses that consensus admits without that condition as central.
rationale: Both identify the same central referent (covenantal/relational knowing vs. mere mental awareness) and share key cases (marital intimacy via Gen 4:1; Lord's acknowledgment via Matt 7:23; obedience link via 1 John 2:3-4). The book preserves this category but materially tightens the boundary and conditions by elevating 'recognized and proven by faithful obedience' into the definition itself, narrowing extension relative to the broader consensus primary meaning and its listed alternatives.
strongest_objection: Consensus treats obedience primarily as evidence or ethical expression of the relational core rather than definitional to it, so the book's tighter formulation may over-narrow what counts as knowing.
